title: The Son
focus: the pain of a father's love

teacherSummary.text: Siddhartha's spoiled son, raised in wealth, despises the ferry life and his father's gentleness. Vasudeva advises letting the boy return to the world, but Siddhartha cannot let go. The son finally runs away, stealing the ferry money. Siddhartha follows to the city and stops at Kamala's old garden, realizing he must not pursue him. Vasudeva brings him home.

context.history: This chapter reverses Chapter One: now Siddhartha is the father whose son leaves.

significance: Siddhartha experiences foolish, painful love—the very attachment he once found childlike.
discussionQuestions: How does Siddhartha's situation mirror his own father's?
Where does characterization appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with love and attachment?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “The Son,” how does Hesse show the pain of a father's love? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how The Son develops the idea of the pain of a father's love. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and irony shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Hermann Hesse uses characterization in The Son to complicate the reader's understanding of the pain of a father's love. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate The Son within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of the pain of a father's love responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads The Son as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of the pain of a father's love. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Siddhartha.

segments.activity: Quick-write and share on the opening question.
segments.script: Good morning, readers. Before we open the book, take three minutes and write your honest answer to this: How does Siddhartha's situation mirror his own father's? There is no wrong answer yet; we will test our ideas against the text today.

segments.activity: Model pronouncing, defining and using five key words in context.
segments.script: Today's words include fornicator, reciprocate, ranting, soiling, burdening. Watch how I figure out a word from its sentence before I check the dictionary. Here is the line: “I hate you, you’re not my father, even if you’ve ten times been my mother’s fornicator!”” My guess comes from the clues around it; the dictionary says: An unmarried person, male or female, who has criminal intercourse with the other sex.

segments.activity: Present background, then the significance of the chapter.
segments.script: Let me give you some background that the first readers of Siddhartha would have known. This chapter reverses Chapter One: now Siddhartha is the father whose son leaves. Now, why does this chapter matter? Siddhartha experiences foolish, painful love—the very attachment he once found childlike. As you listen, jot one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Irony, Theme.
segments.script: Let's read this passage together. I will read the first sentence; you track along. Every time you spot characterization, mark it. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice here? I will collect three ideas on the board and we will choose the strongest one together, using the evidence.
